headline: Niantic Boats Filling Boxes With Fluke and Jumbo Sea Bass — Bass Slide Into the Dark
subhead: Dock talk from Waterford to Niantic says keeper fluke and 28-inch sea bass are stacking the reef structure while the stripers punch the clock after sundown.
body_markdown:
I was standing at the bait shop counter Tuesday morning when one of the Niantic drift boat mates came in for squid and mackerel and just started grinning before I even asked. Said Monday's half-day trip put together a stacked box off Black Point — better than a dozen keeper fluke to 6 pounds and sea bass thick enough that they had a 15-fish limit wrapped up before the second drift was even over. That's the kind of morning that gets the whole fleet buzzing, and it's been the theme all week from Twotree Island Channel out to Hole-in-the-Wall.

The fluke bite has been the most dependable thing going in this zone, and it's holding to the pattern we called last week — the back bay stuff is drying up as the shallow water heats, and the fish are pushing out to the rips, the channel edges, and the reef structure where there's current keeping things cool and stirred up. Black Point and the mouth of Twotree Channel are the spots the party boats keep circling back to, drifting 4-inch white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4 to 1-ounce bucktails, or the old standby — a strip of squid over a 4/0 fluke hook on a fish-finder rig, bounced right along bottom in 25 to 40 feet. Best drifts have been on the stronger stage of the tide, either side of the last hour of the incoming pushing into the top of the high, when there's enough current to keep the bait moving but not so much you're skipping bottom.

Sea bass are honestly stealing some of the fluke's thunder right now. Word out of the Waterford fleet is a 28-inch sea bass came off hard bottom over toward Fishers Island Sound — that's a genuine bull, the kind of fish that makes everybody on the rail start re-tying their rigs mid-trip. Closer to home, McCook Point and the rockpiles off Hole-in-the-Wall have been giving up steady limits of 15-to-18-inch fish on jigs tipped with squid strips, or the classic double-hook porgy rig baited with clam. These fish are locked onto structure and current, not chasing anything around — you want to be dropping straight down on the drift as soon as your fish finder shows relief, and you want weight enough to hold bottom in that current, usually 6 to 10 ounces depending on the stage of tide.

Porgies are mixed right in with the sea bass on that same hard bottom, and if you're fishing bait — clam, squid, sandworms — you're going to catch both in the same drift most days. It's been a nice bonus fishery for anybody targeting sea bass and not minding a mixed bag.

Striped bass are the trickier read right now, and I want to be straight about it. New London's water is sitting around 67.6 degrees, noticeably cooler than what they're dealing with out west in the Sound, but it's still warm enough that the bass in our zone have mostly slid into that nocturnal pattern — feeding hard after dark and holding deep on structure through the heat of the day. The guys working the Niantic River mouth and the deeper edges around Black Point after sundown have been finding fish, working bucktails and soft plastics slow along bottom, or live-lining bunker where you can find pods holding along the current seams. Daytime striper fishing has been a grind — a few fish here and there on the strongest part of the tide around Hole-in-the-Wall, but nothing you'd plan a whole trip around until the sun goes down.

Bluefish have been showing up wherever the bait shows up, which tracks with what's been happening up and down the coast all month — bunker schools pushing into the Sound and the blues stacking right underneath them instead of chasing offshore. If you find a bunker pod pushed up against the current off McCook Point or working the edges of Niantic Bay, there's a good chance there's blues under it, and metal — a Kastmaster or a Deadly Dick worked fast through the school — will get bit in a hurry.

Blackfish are basically off the table right now, which isn't a surprise for mid-July — they've spawned out and scattered off the structure, and nobody's targeting them seriously until the water starts cooling in September.

On the bonito front — we flagged last week that the eastward push of false albacore and bonito would reach this end of the Sound last, and that's exactly how it's playing out. Nothing showing yet from Niantic to Black Point; if there's early scouting fish anywhere, it's going to be out around Montauk or the Vineyard corridor first, and it could be another couple weeks before that shows up on our end.

Looking ahead, the moon's easing toward first quarter on the 21st, which should soften the current stages through the rips over the next few days. That usually means slower presentations produce better on the sea bass and fluke grounds — don't be afraid to downsize your bucktail or slow your drift speed if the tide's not ripping the way it has been. If the stable weather holds, I'd keep hammering the same program: fluke and sea bass during the day on the reef structure, and if you want a shot at stripers, save it for the last two hours of light into full dark around the river mouth and Black Point.
